entries.note: Has long meant influencing events or supernatural forces; from Greek [[from:magos]], related to [[same-root:mage]], literally things associated with the [[same-root:Magi]], short for [[from:ars magica]].
Related to [[same-root:magic]] through Greek magos.
The biblical three wise men, from the plural of Latin magus; also Median and Persian religious specialists in astrology, alchemy and dream interpretation.
The fuller phrase behind [[gave:magic]], meaning the arts associated with the [[see:Magi]].
From French [[from:sorcier]] with a redundant extra -er; ultimately linked to French [[from:sort]], fate or fortune, so a practitioner of fortune.
Medieval Latin term for someone who told fortunes by casting lots, related to [[same-root:sorcerer]].
Telling fortunes by casting lots, now used for mundane random selection such as choosing jurors; related to [[same-root:sortearius]].
From Latin for swearing together, like [[same-root:juror]]; first meant to charge someone by oath, then to bind or compel demons and spirits.
So called because jurors are sworn in, related to [[same-root:conjure]].
The older English word for magic practice, originally not tied to either gender.
From Old English for oath breaker, used of the devil; the -lock is related to [[same-root:lie]], the war- to German [[same-root:wahr]], true; popularised by [[see:Walter Scott]].
Another Old English word with the same liar element as [[see:warlock]].
Shares a Germanic root with the -lock of [[same-root:warlock]].
German for true, cognate with the war- of [[same-root:warlock]].
Writer who popularised Scots words like [[see:warlock]] and [[see:glamour]] in England and, writing much about magic and the past, was called the great magician.
From Old English wicce, feminine of [[from:wicca]], a male sorcerer; the gender-neutral term for practitioners until around the 1600s.
Modern nature-centred pagan religion that took the Old English word for a male witch to give it an ancient feel.
An adjective variation of the Old English word for [[same-root:witch]], making wicked witch redundant.
Old English term for a witch who practised incantations and necromancy.
Another Old English term for a practitioner of incantations and necromancy.
Old English term for a witch who used phantoms and spirits.
Old English term for a witch working with drugs, potions, poisons and charms, from [[from:lyb]], poison or potion.
Spelling once common among many variants; [[see:Aleister Crowley]] revived it around 1912 to separate occult practice from stage [[see:magic]].
Crowley's religious philosophy, named with a Greek word meaning will, choice or desire.
English occultist who popularised [[see:magick]]; a colourful character who inspired fictional characters and much symbolism.
From Latin [[from:cantare]], to sing, like [[same-root:incantation]]: singing something to make it happen.
From Latin [[from:incantare]], already meaning to bewitch, built on cantare, to sing; essentially the same word as [[same-root:enchantment]].
Invokes the same Latin singing verb as [[same-root:enchantment]].
Slang language, previously discussed, also from the Latin for singing, like [[same-root:incantation]].
From Latin [[from:carmen]], song or verse; first a chanted verse, then an object in [[see:Edmund Spenser]]'s The Faerie Queene.
A big song collection whose name is related to [[same-root:charm]].
Common to Germanic languages, originally meaning miracle, but its origin before that is unknown; the state of having witnessed a wonder.
German counterpart of [[same-root:wonder]].
Dutch counterpart of English [[same-root:wonder]].
Swedish counterpart of [[same-root:wonder]].
Danish counterpart of [[same-root:wonder]].
The Romance equivalent of [[see:wonder]], from Latin [[from:miraculum]], an object of wonder, from [[from:mirus]].
Related either to [[same-root?:mirror]] or [[same-root?:miracle]]; a similar Arabic word is a coincidence, the Arabic for mirage being [[see:sarab]].
Spanish verb Rob suspects may connect [[see:miracle]] and [[see:mirage]] to seeing.
A possible relative of [[same-root?:mirage]], fitting since mirages are reflections of the sky.
The standard Arabic word for a desert [[see:mirage]].
Old English for a story or speech, hence a recited magic spell; the letters sense, from the same family, has influence from Old French meaning explain.
Often read as God spell but really good spell, good news, a loan translation of Latin [[from:bona adnuntiatio]]; contains [[same-root:spell]].
From French [[from:grammaire]]; a book on a language's workings, later on other disciplines including magic; a doublet of [[same-root:glamour]].
Scottish form of [[same-root:grammar]] meaning magic, with L and R swapped; spread south via [[see:Walter Scott]]'s fairies using glamour.
Idiom meaning to cast a spell on someone, quoted from The Gypsy Laddie of 1750, before [[see:Walter Scott]].
Ultimately meaning enchanting, from [[from:glamour]] as magic.
A book of spells, exactly the same word as [[same-root:grammar]] and [[same-root:glamour]].
A period of time, unrelated to the magic [[unrelated:spell]]; from Old English for a substitute giving someone rest, then any span, as in cold spell.
Middle English idiom meaning to talk uselessly, using the magic or speech sense of [[see:spell]].
From Dutch [[from:wijsseggher]], soothsayer, folk-etymologised into acre; once a respected prophet, now a know-all; physician [[see:Richard Whitlock]] mocked doctors as wisacres.
Old English for prophet, seer or wise man, a close relative of [[same-root:wiseacre]].
Originally meant understanding or knowledge rather than cleverness; related to [[same-root:wiseacre]] and [[same-root:wise]].
Related to the first element of [[same-root:wiseacre]].
Simply a very wise person, with the intensifying [[see:-ard]]; effectively a doublet of [[same-root:wiseacre]], used from the 15th century.
Jess's favourite ending, an intensifier that is often but not always insulting, as in [[see:drunkard]], [[see:braggart]], [[see:dullard]] and [[see:wizard]].
Someone who drinks too much, an example of [[see:-ard]].
Someone who brags too much, an example of [[see:-ard]].
Something musty, like wine must, seedy and intense in flavour, with the [[see:-ard]] ending.
Someone who is dull, an example of [[see:-ard]].
Invented by [[see:Geoffrey of Monmouth]], who Latinised the Welsh name [[from:Myrddin]] as Merlinus in his telling of King Arthur.
Name of a famous Welsh bard, the source of [[gave:Merlin]]; possibly related to [[same-root?:Mervin]] and [[same-root?:Marvin]].
A name that might be related to [[same-root?:Myrddin]].
A name that might be related to [[same-root?:Myrddin]].
Vectors for divine messages; from [[from:oraculum]], their Roman dwelling, from [[from:orare]], to pray or beseech, not from seeing.
One Greek name for oracles, from a word meaning to declare or proclaim.
Another Greek name for what we call [[see:oracle]]s, meaning seer.
Its spire element refers to breathing in, of spirit and fumes, as [[see:oracle]]s did.
Originally just meant the nature of [[see:oracle]]s.
The place oracles stayed in Rome, from [[from:orare]], to pray or beseech; source of [[gave:oracle]].
From Latin [[from:celare]], to hide, with an assimilated ob-, as in [[same-root:conceal]]; first meant anything secret, later esoteric things.
Essentially to hide together, from the same Latin root as [[same-root:occult]].
Another word with the ob- prefix found in [[see:occult]].
Prefix meaning do again, in Martin's prefix song.
Prefix meaning before, in Martin's prefix song.
Prefix meaning under, in Martin's prefix song.
Prefix meaning not, in Martin's prefix song.
Prefix meaning bad or wrong, in Martin's prefix song.
A concealed part of the house, from the root meaning to cover shared with [[same-root:occult]] and [[same-root:conceal]].
The part that covers you over, from the same root as [[same-root:conceal]].
More or less a Greek [[see:occult]]; from [[from:esoterikos]], belonging to an inner circle, from eso, within.

Origin unclear, possibly [[from?:abecedarius]] or [[from?:Abraxas]]; first in [[see:Quintus Serenus Sammonicus]]'s Liber Medicinalis, written in a shrinking triangle against fever; once meant nonsense.
Pertaining to the alphabet, as in a poem whose lines start with successive letters; a possible source of [[gave?:abracadabra]].
Another magic word, a proposed source of [[gave?:abracadabra]].
Describes a charm meant to turn away disease, danger or evil, like the [[see:abracadabra]] amulet.
Nonsense, once a name for a conjurer; [[see:John Tillotson]] derived it from [[from?:hoc est corpus]], discredited; a 1655 account credits a trickster under James I.
Literally slyness of the hand, from [[from:sleight]]; often misspelled as slight of hand, an eggcorn, but unrelated to [[unrelated:slight]].
Middle English word, variously spelled, meaning craft, cunning or deceptive skill, basically slyness.
Originally flat, smooth or hairless, then slim; to slight someone is to make them small; unrelated to [[unrelated:sleight]].
Recorded as a magic word in the early 1900s; earlier a placeholder for incomprehensible foreign speech, probably mocking Arabs saying Allah.
Magic words from Disney's Cinderella resembling the 1902 [[see:alakazam]] spell, likely inspired by such rhymes.
Anglicised from a [[see:Mandinka]] masked figure who publicly shamed women, per unreliable British accounts; then came to mean superstitious nonsense.
From [[see:Ali Baba]] in the 1001 Nights; sesame is unexplained, perhaps seed pods, oil or a corrupted word; not open says me.
Magic words said by [[see:Matthew Corbett]] or Harry Corbett when [[see:Sooty]] did magic on British children's TV.
Silent yellow magician bear with black ears from British TV, owned by [[see:Matthew Corbett]], inherited from his father Harry.
[[see:Sooty]]'s squeaking dog companion, an agent of chaos whose squeaks were sometimes a little rude.
Italian for quickly; once paired as presto be gone or presto away, then shortened to a magic word, as in [[see:hey presto]].
The familiar magic phrase using [[see:presto]].
Sleight of hand or skilful deception, a French phrase squashed together; in English since Middle English, equivalent to [[equivalent:sleight of hand]].
Sleight of hand, from the older [[from:prestidigitator]].
Coined in 1830 by [[see:Jules de Rovère]] as a grand title, from French [[from:preste]], quick, and Latin [[from:digitus]], finger; echoes Latin [[see:praestigiator]].
French term for a conjurer who makes objects disappear, which [[see:prestidigitator]] was meant to outrank.
French term for performers presenting tricks as demonstrations of natural philosophy and physics.
French for quick or nimble, the root shared with [[same-root:presto]] in [[gave:prestidigitator]].
Latin for a juggler, trickster or deceiver, a predecessor of [[see:prestidigitator]].
Latin for tricks, deceptions or illusions, related to [[same-root:prestige]].
Related to [[from:praestigiae]]; first recorded as an illusion of personal merit, then a reputation for excellence or authority.
Originally practising illusion or full of tricks, derogatory until the 19th century, then ameliorated to having dazzling influence; related to [[same-root:prestige]].
